Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising out of a statement I made in the house last night and which is found on page 4224 of Hansard. We were discussing the provisions of the bill before the house which we thought, in the form in which it was, conflicted with a statement made by the Prime Minister on second reading of the bill, and in a rather colloquial and light-hearted way, in order to point out this conflict and try to have it removed, I said-and I am quoting from Hansard-
All we are asking the minister to do is to make an honest man of the Prime Minister by this amendment.
It has been brought to my attention, Mr. Speaker, that this might be interpreted as a reflection on the Prime Minister. Of course it was not intended as such, and if any such interpretation were given to it I would be the first to regret it.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext:
That on Wednesday, June 3, 1959, and on every Wednesday, Thursday and Friday thereafter until the end of this session, the hours of sitting shall be as follows:
Wednesdays-11:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., and 2:30 p.m. to 6:00 p.m.
Thursdays-11.00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., and 2:30 p.m. to 6:00 p.m., and 8:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m.
Fridays-11:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., and 2:30 p.m. to 6:00 p.m., and 8:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m.; and that the provisions of standing orders 2(1) and 6(3) be suspended In relation thereto.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise simply for the purpose of moving the motion to which you have alluded and to express the hope that it will receive the support of the house. In bringing it up at this point in the session I think we follow in general the position that has been established in this house over the years.
No one will be rash enough to conclude with any certainty the time when the business of the house will be completed in any year. I feel, having regard to the fact that this is the 92nd day of sitting, that it is opportune to do those things which are ordinarily done in order to expedite consideration of the matters yet to be brought before the house.
In presenting the motion I would point out that Mondays and Tuesdays are still left untouched. In that connection may I say that I understand there are still two supply motions to be dealt with before this session can conclude. We are leaving Monday and Tuesday mornings open until the supply motions are dealt with, and at the same time we are providing extra time for the holding of the meetings of committees which are still continuing to sit.
I mentioned a moment ago that I am following a course similar to that taken by my predecessors in office. Looking over the record I find that in 1947 Wednesday evening sittings began on the 78th day, May 28, and that morning sittings-this is one exception I want to place before the house-did not begin until July 10, the 109th day. That was the course as well in 1947-48 when the house opened on December 5 and morning sittings did not begin until the 102nd day.
However, in 1949 the session was divided and at the first session, which was prior to the election, morning sittings began on the 38th day and in the second session following the election on the 42nd day. In the regular session of 1950 the house opened on February 16 and morning sittings began on the 69th day, which was June 1. In 1951 the house opened on January 30 and morning sittings began on June 11, the 88th day. In the second session of 1951 morning sittings began on the 45th day. In the session of 1952

Business of the House
morning sittings began on the 71st day, June 16. In the 1952-53 session morning sittings began on the 84th day. In both 1952-53 and 1953-54 sittings began in the fall of the year and in the 1953-54 session morning sittings began on May 31. In 1955 morning sittings began on June 9, the session having commenced on January 7. In 1956 the session opened on January 10 and morning sittings did not begin until July 16.
Generally speaking this is approximately the time when this motion has been moved. I for one do not want to do anything to place the opposition in an impossible position. I realize how much preparation must be made by an opposition member. I know something of the difficulties involved in not having a secretarial force attached to the civil service to provide the necessary research information. However, taking all these matters into consideration I hope that without in any way indicating that we are trying to rush the conclusion of the session, which is farthest from my mind, I think now is the appropriate time to make this motion. We still have available two mornings in the week, and Saturday sittings do not begin until we are closer to the end than it is apparent at the present time. Wednesday evenings as well are still not taken up.
No one wants to push consideration of the measures that are before the house or which will come before the house. We want the fullest possible discussion, but in order to bring the session to an end within the reasonable period for which we all hope I make this motion at this time, and I am asking for general support.
If on the other hand the attitude is that we do not want to get along, well, the motion will still be in its position on the order paper. However, I hope we can secure that degree of general support which will assure the fullest discussion and the most complete and mature deliberation of the measures that come before us, coupled with that expedition which, I am sure, it is always desired to achieve.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition has asked me to say a word or two on this motion, and I am happy to do so. I am sure that all of us on this side of the house will agree with the general position that it is not only necessary but advisable that we conclude the sittings of this house, having regard however to the amount of work that is before us on the order paper and having regard also to our responsibilities as an opposition to parliament.
I agree with the Prime Minister in some of the suggestions and some of the ideas which

he expressed a moment ago. There are, on the other hand, some matters which I believe should be brought to the attention of parliament and which were perhaps not brought forcibly to the attention of the Prime Minister. Some of them are as follows. In the first place, I think the moment this motion is put on the order paper it is indicative that the end of the session is in sight. This has been my experience, at least, when I sat on the other side of the house. However, when I look at the order paper, and when I look at the estimates unpassed, and at the work of the committees, as well as some of the other things which I will mention later, I cannot see the end of this session in sight before anywhere from six to eight weeks, or perhaps more than that.
I shall tell the Prime Minister why. All one has to do is glance at the order paper and at the other matters with which parliament is concerned. The first of these is the estimates. Thus far only three departments have been concluded, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, the Department of Agriculture, and I believe the Department of Labour. All the other departments still remain to be dealt with. I am not suggesting for one moment that the other departments should take as long as these three. I hope they will not. We will certainly give the fullest co-operation to the consideration of these estimates with the dispatch which is necessary to their proper consideration.
But I remind the house that the remaining departments alone constitute enough work for almost four weeks, if not more than that. Then from amongst those departments I single out the Department of National Defence which is one which certainly should take as much time, because of its importance, as the Department of Agriculture. There is the Department of External Affairs, upon which we have had some debate but which has not been completed. There are many other departments, including the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I am sure my friend the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) will have a long statement to make which will be highly contentious-

subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext: There is nothing contentious in it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext: -and which will take some time. But be that as it may, there are these estimates which deserve consideration. Then there is the work of the committees. It seems to me that the practice in the past has been to bring in a motion of this kind when the work of the committees was about completed or on the verge of being completed. My understanding of the work of the committees is that it has hardly begun.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext:
My hon. friends say "Oh, oh". Let them look at Votes and Proceedings of yesterday. There, on the last page but one, they will see what committees are meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday of this week. There are no less than eight such committees meeting. How we can perform our duties in the House of Commons and be at those committees is rather difficult to understand, particularly now when the house is going to sit in the mornings beginning on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. It therefore seems to me that little or no consideration has been given to that fact.
Then I am informed by the hon. member for Essex East that in the committee on industrial relations a motion was made, which fortunately was not passed; at least an attempt was made to have that committee sit while the house was sitting. That is a repetition of what was done in the public accounts committee last year. Although the attempt was made it was not successful. I submit that this procedure is a mistake. With deference I submit to the Prime Minister that it is a mistake to ask the members of the opposition while we are responsible for our work in the house, to sit in committees while the house is sitting and to consider matters of importance in those committees.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext: Why don't you work?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext:
It seems to me that procedure is not consistent with the work we have to perform in the house. Then all I need say in response to those on the other side of the house who are interrupting, is to ask them to remember what attitude was taken by those who now sit on the government benches under similar circumstances when they sat on this side of the house. I know they protested bitterly under those circumstances. Having regard to the information I have just given here, I do not see that the circumstances are at all different.
Then, Mr. Speaker, would you allow me to say a word about the legislation which remains to be dealt with by the house. The Leader of the Opposition asked the Prime Minister-I believe it was on April 21 of this year-what the remaining business was. Just listen to this, 'Mr. Speaker; this is what the Prime Minister said six weeks ago, as reported at page 2877 of Hansard:
I would say that in addition to the items which are already on the order paper the following will be introduced: the bill of rights, a bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, a bill to establish a national energy board, a bill to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act, a bill to provide additional grants to the province of Newfoundland, an amendment to the Bretton Woods Agreements Act; bills respecting the superannuation of members of the
Business of the House
Royal Canadian Mounted Police and members of the Canadian forces; a bill to amend the Combines Investigation Act, and a bill to bring in certain amendments to the Criminal Code.
Then he went on to say this:
In the field of agriculture, amendments will be introduced to assist the provinces in implementing crop insurance, as well as a bill to extend and improve farm credit facilities, and a bill to allow veteran farmers to take greater advantage of modern agricultural practices will be introduced by way of amendment to the Veterans Land Act.
In addition there will be, of course, the budget legislation-
Which, of course, has been disposed of.
-and the usual measure respecting the financing of the Canadian National Railways. Consideration is also being given to certain other measures of lesser importance.
Much of the legislation appearing in the list I have just mentioned is contentious, and the vast majority of it is still not before the house. The only items mentioned in this list which are now before the house are the bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, which is under consideration by a committee, and the bill which is now under consideration in this house to establish a national energy board. All the rest-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext: And the Bretton Woods Agreement Act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Yes. I agree there are some non-contentious matters which I have not time to deal with, such as the one the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has just mentioned. That matter is entirely non-contentious, and I can assure the minister at once that we will give the fullest co-operation to that matter in its passing. In addition to that, sir, there are two motions to go into supply. They may take two days, they may take one day, I do not know; that will be a matter for the house to determine.
What I deprecate in particular is this. If this legislation which was announced by the Prime Minister six weeks ago, much of it contentious, is brought down now, this legislation, a lot of it important, will be brought down in the last days of the session. I refer particularly to the federal-provincial taxsharing agreements. There is an example of an agreement upon which there has been a good deal of debate, that is true; but it seems to me that is a matter which should not under normal conditions take the time it has taken.
I say this to the government, with respect. I believe in my mind and in my heart that it is not the intention of the government to change in any way the formula that was established in that legislation. That being the case, why is it necessary to renew this agreement each year? Why is it not possible by one piece of legislation to dispose of it in one

Business of the House
session? That is why I say it is a contentious matter which comes before parliament each year.
I presume I will be told after I have resumed my seat that we take far too much time in discussing the matters which from time to time come before the house. But let me assure my hon. friends opposite that members on the government side also take up a great deal of time. I am not complaining about that; that is their right and their privilege. However, I can point to two or three debates where they did take up a great deal more time than we on this side of the house. That being the case I do not think complaint can be made that we are taking undue length of time.
In my opinion, sir, this motion is premature. It seems to me that the motion is aimed at ending the sittings of this house by a fixed date. I may be wrong in that assumption; if I am, then I will accept the correction. But what I think the house should be reminded of is that we on this side have a job to do. We feel that that job cannot be done within a few weeks. We feel that because of the legislation, contentious as much of it is, announced by the Prime Minister, because of the remaining departments which have not even yet been touched, and because of the committee work, most of which has not been reported upon, this motion is, as I say, premature.
I do hope the Prime Minister will accept these remarks in the spirit in which he made his opening remarks a moment ago. With that in mind I ask the Prime Minister if he will not give consideration to this suggestion, because I am sure that when he rose a while ago he rose with no other intention but that of being helpful. At least that is what I gathered from the tone of his remarks.
The suggestion I make is that until the majority of the committees have reported on their work for this session, this motion should be allowed to stand on the order paper. If that were done I am sure there would be a greater disposition on the part of those of us who sit on this side of the house to find ourselves in agreement with the government on a motion such as this at this stage of the session.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is true to say that this is approximately the usual stage during a session when a motion is brought forward to provide for morning sittings. However, I do believe that at least some hon. members in this house are slightly in error in their thinking and in their hope that being a member of parliament is really just a part time job. It seems to me

that as the nation expands and parliament has to deal each session with an increasing volume of legislation, the fact becomes more and more clear that being a member is a full time job.
If this is the case I think we should attempt to get away from the practice of trying to cram the work of the session into five or six consecutive months. Rather, the government in consultation with other parties in the house should consider whether or not the business of parliament can be more efficiently dealt with by a longer session and more frequent recesses. This would, of course, have the advantage of permitting the employees of the building, the members of the staff and the members of the House of Commons, to enjoy holidays during the summer months, which is the normal time when holidays are taken by most Canadians.
I also think that in closing the debate the Prime Minister should inform the house as to whether or not there are new pieces of legislation to be advanced during this session and, in general, whether there is to be any greater work load given parliament than we have been told about heretofore.
In fairness I should also say that this motion to a substantial degree is a compromise motion. It is not a motion to call for morning sittings five days a week, nor does it call for evening sittings five days a week or on Saturdays. Instead it is asking that parliament sit Wednesday and Thursday mornings as well as Friday evenings in addition to the regular hours of sitting. At this particular stage of the session and in view of the attitude of the parties generally as to how sessions should be managed, we feel this is an appropriate time to bring forward a motion of this nature.
We wish to point out, however, in the strongest possible terms that there is an excellent argument for those who say that committees of the house should not sit while the house is sitting. We know that certain committees are sitting when the house is sitting. I believe there should be a reluctance on the part of the members of all committees that are not now sitting while the house is sitting to accept this extra burden, at least for another couple of weeks until we see how the session progresses.
The greatest objection to this motion arises from the possibility that after this motion passes there might be a further endeavour to have more committees meet while the house is sitting. This would make the work of all hon. members of parliament completely impossible, and would bring parliament into critical view on the part of the Canadian public.

With these reservations and with the hope that the Prime Minister will give consideration to the suggestion we have made, we are prepared to give this motion our support.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is very little for me to add to what my colleague has said, but it seems to me the consideration that weighs most in our minds is the difficulty of combining committee work when there is so much of it in progress, with our duties in the House of Commons. The Prime Minister himself earlier in the session said it was not his intention to make impossible the reconciliation of the duties of committee members with their duties in the house, but with eight or nine committees sitting and with some of them sitting more than once a day it is extremely difficult if not impossible for members of the official opposition to do full justice to their work in the committees and in the house.
Having regard to what he said earlier in the session about this matter I would therefore ask the Prime Minister if he would not be fair enough to have another look at this situation next month in the light of the progress made by the committees, and if the progress that has been made is satisfactory a motion of this kind would surely be more acceptable to all hon. members of the house then than it is now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to thank all hon. gentlemen for the contributions they have made to the discussion of this very important matter. I fully understand the position that is advanced by the hon. member for Laurier. To summarize his words, he said there might be some who say we spend too much time discussing matters that come before the house. I do not belong to that school, nor have I ever adhered to the suggestion that beneficial discussion shall not take place on every measure that comes before the house.
Sometimes I think all of us are prone to error in that regard, in believing that prolixity and repetition take the place of full and careful consideration and deliberation on the matters that come before the house, but the latter is of the essence in the discharge of the responsibilities of parliament. I wish to do nothing that would in any way reduce the opportunity of those in the opposition to engage in the fullest discussion, nor do I wish to coerce the opposition in any way.
I was very impressed by the views expressed by the hon. member for Assiniboia. The group he represents is small in number, and naturally members of that group have
Business of the House
a variety of matters to discuss that would tax the energies of a group three or four times the size of the one in question.
In general our viewpoint is that we do want the fullest possible consideration. I do not want to be in the position of pressing upon the opposition the acceptance of this motion. The hon. member for Laurier said it looks like six weeks and possibly more. It is the responsibility of parliament to discuss and consider these matters to the full. There is no question of a target date such as he suggested. I for one would not to the slightest degree concur in any suggestion that we determine upon a target date and thereby fail to do what is required of us, so we can banish that thought.
Of course, whether the house takes until September is an open question. When sitting in opposition I was told that the length of the session is always determined by the opposition. The entire field of legislation has been set out, in so far as it is possible to do so, in the outline referred to by the hon. member for Laurier. Some matters may arise that at the moment cannot be contemplated, but with due regard to that possibility I may say that that which was set out some weeks ago represents the program of legislation which will be submitted to parliament.
Mention was made of the difficulty of attending committees while the house was sitting. This motion, as the hon. member for Assiniboia has said, is a compromise one. Instead of going the whole way, as has been the custom in the past, of providing in the beginning for sittings in the mornings throughout the week and on Friday nights, to begin with, the only possible interference with committees would be on Wednesday and Thursday. We will not sit on Wednesday evenings. Committees do not sit on Wednesday evenings or on Friday evenings; at least it was not my experience throughout the years that there was ever any desire for committees to sit particularly on Friday evenings.
However, hon. gentlemen opposite have taken very strong objection, as I say, to the course suggested. I think it would tend to meet the needs of the opposition to assure them that in every way they will have the fullest possible opportunity to thoroughly discuss the measures that will be brought before the house. The hon. member for Laurier, speaking for the official opposition, has taken a very strong stand on this.
I am not going to be put in the position of having a vote forced on the house and thereby the opposition take the stand that if it had not come to a vote things might have been different. The C.C.F. group are prepared to support this; the official opposition are not.

Business of the House
In the circumstances, therefore, I am going to suggest that we might possibly come to an agreement whereby in this motion, if the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Assiniboia would agree, we might alter the date from June 3 to June 10, thereby enabling both sides to get together; because I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I am not going to adopt the attitude that has been adopted in years past by which the majority in a matter such as this has been pitted against the opposition. I suggest an alternative in the spirit which was apparent in the remarks of the hon. member for Laurier.
By leave of the house I would ask, providing there is going to be support in that direction, that the amendment be made accordingly.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, seeing that the Prime Minister has suggested that the motion might be changed, perhaps I can say an additional word. The suggestion made by the Prime Minister is that the date of the motion should be postponed from June 3 to June 10. In the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, this seems to me a reasonable compromise between the two points of view that were put forward this afternoon. I would ask the Prime Minister, in stating our agreement with this change, that everything possible be done to ensure that committee work should not be of a type and held at times which would make it impossible for members on this side to do their whole duty in the House of Commons itself. I mention that to the Prime Minister because he himself mentioned it this afternoon. I know it is in his mind. Perhaps I should also add that we are assuming, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister is not proposing to bring in additional legislation at this stage.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext: I want to be clear on this. I have not anything in mind nor has any member of the government; but the hon. gentleman knows from his experience in the cabinet that there are occasions when matters arise which require attention. Should such a matter or matters arise they will be kept to a minimum, but I know of none at the moment that could arise. I would not expect that anyone would suggest that there is a complete undertaking that those eventualities should not be taken cognizance of today.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON WEDNESDAYS, THURSDAYS AND FRIDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I quite understand there may be an emergency which will require legislation. I would not try to suggest to the Prime Minister that that might not happen. All I am doing is mentioning those two difficulties. Having mentioned them, I am quite willing to tell the Prime Minister that as far as we are concerned the change he has suggested in this motion is satisfactory.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are prepared to accept this compromise suggested by the Prime Minister. I think it is a good move by the Prime Minister, since apparently it is obtaining the acceptance of the official opposition. We would like to urge two things; one, all legislation that the government intends to introduce at this time should be put before parliament immediately; two, there should be no move within the next week, until at least June 10, to provide that any further committees of the house in fact sit while the house is sitting. If we can have this further period when no additional committees are meeting while the house is sitting and have a chance to see all the proposed legislation as soon as possible, we think these things will expedite the business of the house.

Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Transport and ask him whether he is aware of the statement which is reported in the morning's press by the Montreal tourist and convention bureau, which is a very strong organization in the city of Montreal, concerning the airport at Dorval, in which it is said that the federal government alone is responsible for the delay in finishing the new terminal building at Montreal. Has the minister seen this report, and would he care to comment on it?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Laurier directed a question to my colleague the Minister of Transport, relating to fines levied against two air lines at Gander for infraction of the quarantine regulations. This matter comes within my jurisdiction and I feel that my department's position should be made clear.
I can appreciate the air lines' desire to have their passengers go through quarantine inspection as quickly as possible, but for the protection of the public adequate arrangements must be made. The procedure adopted now that the new terminal is operating has not been criticized by most of the air lines and, in fact, is essentially the same as at major airports all over the world.
Difficulties centre around the refusal of pilots of certain air lines to arrange to have their passengers escorted into the terminal for clearance and customs by the route provided. This is their responsibility, and by their failure to co-operate they have caused a great deal of confusion for their own passengers and others using the terminal. Infractions were repeatedly pointed out by my officers, and as no improvement was forthcoming fines were levied against two air line companies.
I trust that as airport routine settles down, following the problems that were only to be expected with the start of operations in the new building, the air lines will be able to organize a more effective procedure.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak to the amendment which is before the committee to clause 85, subclause 2. In the discussion of this clause, which is an exemption clause, yesterday the hon. member for Essex East said this, as reported at page 4229 of Hansard, when he was criticizing what he called a far-reaching clause:
Yet this present government, with less than two years in office, comes to parliament and puts before us a clause like this, the like of which perhaps no government in the history of Canada has ever tried to put before parliament.
I should like to draw attention to the fact that this type of exemption clause is not unfamiliar to the House of Commons. In 1955, when the hon. member for Essex East was a member of the government of that day, a meat inspection act was before the house; it is chapter 36 of the statutes of 1955. In it under the heading of "Regulations" there was a section, namely section 5, which reads in part as follows:
5. The governor in council may make regulations for carrying out the purposes and provisions of this act, and without limiting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations-

Then I read subparagraph (g) which is as follows:
(g) for exempting any person or meat product from the operation of all or any of the provisions of this act-
According to the argument of my hon. friend last night this destroys the act in whole. Then in the same year-

speechtext: What was the chapter?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
That was chapter 36 of the statutes of 1955. Then I have another reference for my hon. friend. It is chapter 47 in the same book of statutes, which is the International River Improvements Act. Section 3 of that act, dealing with regulations, reads as follows:
3. The governor in council may, for the purpose of developing and utilizing the water resources of Canada in the national interest, make regulations-
Then I read subparagraph (d) which is as follows:
(d) excepting any international river improvements from the operation of this act.
In the hon. member's argument that means that the act is destroyed by that exemption.
Then just to refresh his memory further may I draw attention to an act which, when I mention it, will perhaps stimulate his memory. I refer to the Food and Drugs Act, being chapter 38 of the statutes of Canada, 1952-53, introduced into this house by the then minister of national health and welfare, our genial friend the hon. member for Essex East. As he piloted that bill through the house he came across, under the heading "Regulations", section 24, which reads as follows:
24. (1) The governor in council may make regulations for carrying the purposes and provisions of this act into effect, and, in particular, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations-
Then I go to paragraph (j):
(j) exempting any food, drug, cosmetic or device from all or any of the provisions of this act and prescribing the conditions of such exemption;-
That bill was introduced into and passed by the House of Commons under the direction of the hon. member for Essex East, who now tells us that never before had a clause such as that which we have in this bill been put before the House of Commons. He himself put similar clauses before the House of Commons and they were passed by the house.
Then in the course of his argument the hon. member talked about the regulations. I dealt with that matter last night, but for the purpose of clarity may I repeat that the regulations by law, under the Regulations
National Energy Board Act, must be printed in the Canada Gazette and subsequently tabled in the House of Commons, a fact of which the hon. member was quite aware. When the debate was taking place on April 21, 1953, on the Food and Drugs Act, when the question was asked him about the regulations, as reported at page 4150 of Hansard he replied as follows-

National Energy Board that amendment is moved to clause 87 the hon. member who has moved the present amendment, which is to strike out the new one, of course is at liberty to move a further amendment. As the person who moved the original amendment I wish to thank the minister for the consideration the government has given to our contention that this paragraph should be deleted. We are extremely happy that the government is so moving. We shall take a look at the proposed amendment to clause 87 of the bill when we reach it. We feel-and I repeat what I have said before-that far too often throughout this bill the governor in council has maintained a power of veto, a power to set aside any regulations or any decisions of the board and to substitute therefor decisions and regulations of the cabinet.
We think that in general this is a bad procedure. Anything that will reduce the power of the cabinet to make a plaything of the board is most acceptable to us. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure my hon. friend recognizes from what has been said already what satisfaction we derive from his acceptance of the argument we made last night. I can only say that what the minister has done now is consistent with what he called, as far as I am concerned, an argument with which I was carried away. However, that argument, along with observations made by others, has obviously had the kind of effect which we thought in the circumstances it should have on the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Reference was made to the Food and Drugs Act and to the section-section 16, I presume [DOT]-where the board is given power subject to the approval of the governor in council to make regulations. I am afraid the minister can hardly consider the Food and Drugs Act and what was done under section 16 as in any way a parallel to the complaint registered last night by me. In any event, assuming that my hon. friend's argument was correct,


and assuming I had been guilty of the very act I complained about last night, this would not of course in any way preclude me from taking the position I am taking now, any more than it precluded the hon. gentleman from taking a particular position in 1955 in connection with one of the many debates to which he made reference a few moments ago.
I have had the opportunity since we met last night of reading not only the observations of some of my hon. friend's colleagues in that debate, but more particularly the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he sat on this side as a private member of this house. In comparing what he said on that occasion with what I said last night I note a similarity of theme. But I congratulate the minister because he spoke about that theme much better, and I am sure with even greater force and fervour, than I did last night.
In any event, perhaps I may recall his words to him, because I realize his preoccupation with this bill and with other matters, and he has not had an opportunity of rereading his words. I think at a time like this where we are discussing such an important measure the minister would want to be reminded of words which my humble researches have disclosed. At page 4688 of Hansard for June 13, 1955, almost at the top of the page I find these words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. They apply forcefully at the present time because we have so many new members in this house. The minister said:
I think it is incumbent upon the senior members of the house to be the foremost to defend the parliamentary system, to exercise moderation with respect to any suggested changes, and to restrain newcomers to the house when they appear to be impatient with the parliamentary system.
That was very good advice in 1955, and undoubtedly last night I was suffering somewhat from an impatience to see that our parliamentary system was not in any way violated.

I have not heard what my hon. friend said, but I am sure it will bear waiting and I will read it in Hansard tomorrow. Further down on the same page the minister said:
Actually he is attempting to reverse the process. Normally ministers come to parliament and ask for extension of their powers or for special powers for

special purposes and parliament examines the situation, makes the grant of power and withdraws it when the crisis has subsided.
There is another quotation, but I will not put it on the record at this time as there may be some opportunity later on, unless my hon. friend finds it desirable to take the proper course which he has just announced.
Before I take my seat I can only say to my hon. friend that I have no doubt that the value of discussion, the value of persuasion and debate, has had its effect today as a result of the insistent position taken by members of the opposition last night, who looked upon this particular subclause 2 in clause 85 as one that violated our concept of what was the proper relationship between the executive and parliament. That my hon. friend has accepted our proposal is, I say, the best demonstration one could have of the value of parliament and of the opportunity of continued free discussion, and of the recognition by the executive of its obligation and its traditional constitutional relationship to parliament itself.

Mr. Chairman, I also want to express my pleasure at the agreement of the minister to the amendment. As I indicated yesterday, the people in the lower mainland of British Columbia have been very much concerned for some considerable time now at the realization that natural gas was being exported and supplied to United States wholesalers at a lower price than was being charged for the same product to our own British Columbia consumers. Representations were made to the royal commission on energy, and the royal commission has roundly condemned the practice of the Westcoast Transmission Company.

There is another point in connection with this clause that I want to raise. Perhaps I should read the relevant part of the clause before making my argument. The clause now reads:
The governor in council may make regulations for carrying into effect the purposes and provisions of this part and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations respecting (b) the duration of licences, not exceeding 25 years, the quantities that may be exported or imported under licences and any other terms or conditions to which licences may be subject.
The point I want to deal with is that under the existing legislation it has been the practice to limit the duration of licences for the export of electricity to one year. I believe that to be a fact. Of course, permits for the exportation of gas are not limited as to time, as I understand it, or at least they do not terminate after a year. There may be some correction in that regard but that is my understanding of the present method of issuing export licences.
With respect to gas, however, because of the nature of the product and in order to finance the enterprise and indeed to have the type of contract we want entered into it is probably necessary that an export permit be for a longer duration than one year. But as to electricity, I am somewhat concerned with granting the power to grant licences for a longer period at one time than one year.
As was clearly illustrated in the discussion last night on another clause by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the electric power that is usually exported is surplus power. I can see no consideration that would arise that would demand that licences for the export of electrical energy be for a longer period than one year. Indeed, with respect to electric power there is a danger of having electricity exported from Canada which we should be using as a basis for our own development, instead of merely exporting the surplus which by the nature of the product is not likely to be nearly as extensive as in the case of gas.
The export permit for electricity is incidental to the development and operation of the plant for the use of Canadians whereas the export of gas in certain areas may be a major undertaking in its own right, the rights and interests of Canadians having been protected through other means by gas supplied from other areas.

One way to assure development of Canadian industry of course, is the permit for the export of such gas, bearing in mind that the protection of the Canadian interest is assured by supply from other areas, but no such case or argument exists when we are dealing with hydroelectric energy. I therefore propose moving an amendment to provide for the limitation of the electricity export permit to one year. Before doing so, I want to know whether the minister has any real case to make for the change in the practice with respect to the export of electrical energy?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is well that the hon. member for Ottawa West has raised this question because it is an important one. He is quite right. For many years now electrical power exports have been on the basis of annual export licences. I anticipate that that will be the case with regard to most of our hydroelectric stations in Canada where surplus power goes across the border. At the present time in quantity it is very limited. Six per cent of the total amount of hydroelectric power produced in Canada is exported, and exported on the basis of an annual licence. But there are two developments which are likely to take place in the future which might change that picture. I think there would be a great reluctance on the part of the energy board to grant a licence for more than the present arrangement of one year unless some very large development of electric power took place, as could happen out in western Canada. The negotiations taking place now with regard to the Columbia river is a case in point. There might be an arrangement between the two countries where in exchange for some advantage to Canada electrical power produced on that great river system might be exported to the United States on a licence basis longer than one year.
The second development which might take place in the future is in thermal power plants which might, using coal in Alberta, in British Columbia or in other provinces in Canada, produce electricity for export beyond the requirements in Canada. These are two things which might influence the energy board to grant licences longer than on a one-year basis. Then, in connection with either of the two possibilities that I have mentioned, for financing purposes a guarantee extending over a 20 or 25-year period of export of electricity might be necessary if the company were to become operative. That is the reason for not making the section here restrictive in so far as hydroelectric power is concerned.

National Energy Board seems to me that there is such a great danger of the hydroelectric power being alienated from the use of Canada through the grant of a long term export licence that we should have some restriction on it. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, ordinarily I
would not take part in the discussion of this bill as it is being put through the house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. However, the amendment raises a point which is of vital importance to the province of British Columbia and if it should carry it might be disastrous to that province. The position at the moment with regard to the Columbia is that after many years of wrangling and of impossibility of getting within any distance at all of agreement with the United States concerning the development of power on the Columbia river we have now been able to make great strides.
Hon. members will remember that in December of last year I made a statement as acting prime minister concerning the possibility of reaching agreement with the United States, and in that statement it was suggested that the international joint commission should be given the task of working out the details of an agreement for the payment of downstream benefits arising out of power developed on that river. The United States government agreed to this suggestion and for some months now the commission has been working very well in the direction of reaching an agreement on the payment of downstream benefits.
Not only has there been co-operation between Canada and the United States but there has also been excellent co-operation between the federal government and the provincial government. A policy committee has been established on the ministerial level between the two governments. That committee met in Ottawa some weeks ago and it met again in Victoria on Friday last. The two federal ministers on that committee are the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and myself. Unfortunately I was unable to go west for the last meeting. But they had another good meeting at which the ministers and officials of both governments co-operated in a splendid spirit to work out the proposals that should be submitted on behalf of Canada to the international joint commission. I believe there has been a meeting of the international joint commission within the last two or three days. I believe they met in New York on May 31.
Fundamental in this whole question is that Canada shall get back power produced in the United States as downstream benefits for the storage of water upstream on the Columbia river in British Columbia. This is where the cheapest power will come from. I would say that power cannot be produced in any other

way anywhere on the North American continent that will compete with it as to price. What position are we going to be in if we write into our statute that Canada can give an export permit only for one year and yet we are expecting to get power back from the United States by way of downstream benefits? They will write into their law just as tight a restriction as we write into our law and this very provision, if it should be accepted by the house, might very well be taken by the United States authorities as being an attempt to hamper negotiations or to cut down on the terms of any agreement. That is a position in which Canada simply cannot afford to be put.
This is the biggest development that has ever been possible in the province of British Columbia. It is a huge development which will involve the expenditure of perhaps a billion dollars in Canada when all of the projects have been installed. But the very foundation on which this development rests is downstream benefits from the plants on the Columbia in the United States of America, and I do suggest that to put in an amendment of this kind would be most unwise.
Furthermore, this works both ways. There is a plant owned by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company on the Pend Oreille river, a tributary of the Columbia, just a few miles north of the border. Why they built that plant there I never could understand when there was such a prohibition against exporting power. There they have a large plant and there is a possibility of a big increase in the size of the plant. All the possible installations have not been made, and sooner or later some of that power will have to be exported to the United States. It is produced because of storage on the Pend Oreille river in the United States. That river rises in the United States and flows through Canada for a few miles. In those few miles this plant has been built, so that there you have exactly the opposite position to that which you find on the main stem of the river.
When all these projects on the Columbia are installed power may have to be exported from other Canadian plants, say at Mica creek. Should there be a big power project installed there I doubt whether all the power would be required in British Columbia at that time. Some of it might have to be exported to the United States for the time being.
The Conservative party is the last party in the country to want to adopt any policy which would be against Canada's interests in so far as dealings with the United States are concerned. The whole history of the party proves that, but in this case I submit it would be folly to adopt the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Ottawa West. I 66968-9-270
National Energy Board realize that he puts it forward with the best of motives, but he puts it forward without an understanding of the facts of life in 1959 in the western part of Canada.

The hon. member is quite right in saying that the Canadian people and parliament have been very jealous with regard to their rights concerning the export of electricity. That statement is true. I have read the story of electricity over the last fifty years. Parliament has taken extreme care to see that there was no carelessness in the export of electricity to the disadvantage of Canada.
The hon. member for Ottawa West was incorrect in stating that the annual licence was in legislation and that we were now changing legislation by this clause in the bill that is before us. That is not so. In the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act there is nothing that restricts the export of electric power to one year. It is part of the regulations.
May I say one further word. Although there has been a good deal of discussion with regard to the development of hydroelectric power, I mentioned the fact-and I want to emphasize it again-that there is great opportunity ahead of Canada in the development of electric power by thermal stations 66968-9-270J
National Energy Board using our abundant supplies of coal. The financing of that proposition is like the financing of a gas pipe line or an oil pipe line. It must be on a long term basis, extending over twenty years or twenty-five years. Unless the authority is given to the national energy board to have licences running up to twenty-five years it seems to me that a development such as the one I have heard about could not take place. We are expecting that they will be just as careful as Canadians have been in the last fifty years with the export of our power resources and that they will be just as careful as any member of this chamber would be.
