subtopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howard for the second reading of Bill No. C-13, to amend the Canada Elections Act.

subtopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROTECT VOTING RIGHTS OF INDIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the mover of this bill had in mind taking it as an adjunct to Bill No. C-15, to amend the Indian Act, because the purpose of Bill No. C-13 is in effect to take out of the present provisions of the Canada Elections Act those restrictions which presently exist in so far as they prohibit an Indian as defined in the Indian Act from casting his vote at a federal election.
On June 10, 1958 a somewhat similar bill designed to amend the Indian Act was before the house and I made certain remarks in connection with our consideration of that bill which I submit to the house showed that the amendments sought thereunder were impossible of implementation because they had not considered deeply enough the legal status, in effect, of the Indian people whom the legislation was intended to affect.
I think it important for the house to consider before passing on this legislation just

Canada Elections Act
what is the legal status of an Indian. The Indian Act is chapter 149 of the revised statutes. Under this act an Indian is defined as a person who pursuant to the act is registered as an Indian or is entitled to be registered as an Indian. In section 5 the Indian Act sets forth that an Indian register shall be maintained by the department which shall consist of band lists and general lists in which there shall be recorded the name of every person who is entitled to be registered as an Indian.
A qualification to the definition of an Indian can be found in section 12, subsection 1, paragraph (b) of the Indian Act. There it is set forth that a woman who is married to a person who is not an Indian is not entitled to be registered as an Indian. Under section 14 of the act a woman who is a member of the band ceases to be a member of that band if she marries a person who is not a member of the band; in other words, if she marries either a white person or a person who is an Indian entitled to be registered but in another band. The point I wish to make in this regard is that an Indian woman who marries a white person ceases to be a person registered as an Indian upon marriage. When her husband dies, however, her status could well be argued to revert.
The explanatory notes of Bill No. C-15 read as follows:
The purpose of this bill is complementary to another bill of this session to amend the Canada Elections Act. It is to provide that Indians, as defined in this act-
I submit that those words are important, "as defined in this act". I continue:
-shall be entitled to vote at federal elections without detracting from their hereditary, treaty, aboriginal, or other similar rights.
In order for this suggested legislation to have effect at all the Indian whom it purports to touch must be an Indian as defined in the Indian Act. I have attempted to show that the definition as it presently stands in the Indian Act falls somewhat short of being an all-inclusive definition.
In that regard the companion legislation, Bill No. C-17, does not by its provision cover this eventuality. In considering what is the legal status of a Canadian Indian it should be pointed out that not all so-called Canadian Indians have special legal status as Indians. I have already attempted to show that in order to have that status an Indian must be registered with the federal Indian affairs department in accordance with the provisions of the Indian Act as it now stands.
There are three groups of so-called Indian people in Canada who are not eligible to be

registered at all and therefore do not have Indian status. They are the Indians whose ancestors have left the Indian reserve or who do not have a residential status on the reserve; the Indians who have mixed blood in their veins-and of course we are not concerned with this group in our discussion- and married women who by reason of marrying away from a band cease to be regarded as Indians.
Those persons who are not registered as Indians have a great many problems both socially and financially and very unhappy problems they are, too. The courts through the years have held that when these Indians are off the reserve the laws of the dominion and the province shall apply to them, while on the reserve the laws of the dominion and the province shall apply unless they are in direct conflict with the rights given by a treaty or by the Indian Act itself. I shall attempt to show the nature of this problem if hon. members will bear with me.
Both by treaty and by the Indian Act the Indian is given a legal status which is inferior to that of the ordinary Canadian citizen. Perhaps this is just as opportune a time as any to say that the hon. member who moved this bill certainly has my full support because the principle he is seeking to have established through the bill is a proper one. The Indian is just as much if not more a Canadian citizen than any of us and certainly the right to vote in a federal election should be his. The Eskimo people should also have the inalienable right to vote.
There are approximately 165,000 treaty Indians in Canada today according to a recent count, one-half of whom live in eastern Ontario. This entire group is a minority in our midst and as I said the Indians suffer from a greatly inferior legal status. I submit that the blame for this situation does not lie entirely with the white man alone; the red man, the Canadian Indian, is just as responsible for his lack of adequate legal status today. This is a product of history and in order to examine why this is so I propose to refer to some of that history very briefly.
The French by the Treaty of Capitulation of 1760 and the Treaty of Paris in 1763 admitted the Indians' claims to hunting rights and to land. In 1790 the English began taking surrenders of land from the Indians, paying money and wampum for these lands. In 1792 Governor Simcoe surrendered a crown grant of land to the Indians of the Six Nations in return for a surrender of a large area of land over which that tribe had dominance. In eastern Canada these capitulations and exchanges of land were called "surrenders",

and in some cases were crown grants. In other cases the title was held for the Indians by the crown.
That is pretty well the situation today. The Indians signed the treaty expecting the justice of the white man's chief and instead they were to find the restrictive laws of Canada were to apply to them but not those guaranteeing them legal status as Canadians in all of the implications of that latter phrase.
By the treaty he had been made a ward of the crown, and he could obtain land, but not land held in fee simple, outright. He could earn a livelihood by hunting. There is much concern, as suggested by the mover of this bill, as to whether the treaty rights have been upheld. The Indian has the right to hunt. The federal government, under the British North America Act, had exclusive jurisdiction as to Indians. However, the federal government transferred its resources in 1930 to the provinces, and with this went the jurisdiction over hunting and fishing rights. The Indians were charged by game wardens and others in charge of resources for hunting without a permit and hunting out of season. Most of those cases were undefended and the Indians were levied pretty hefty fines. Today, this is not the situation, as is evidenced by a recent decision in the case of an Eskimo at any rate by a judge of the territorial court of the Northwest Territories. In any event, suffice it to say the courts today uphold those long preserved treaty rights of the Indians.
The right of occupation of certain areas of land, now commonly known as Indian reserves, has not been diminished in so far as those having treaty rights are concerned. At the time of the signing of the treaties to which I referred great emphasis was placed on the fact that this land was preserved to be available to the Indian and his children and his children's children. It was a great inducement to the Indian people at the time to sign the treaty. Under those treaties the Indians obtained an inferior legal status. I will come back to this point again.
To revert for a moment, may I say that that particular status in effect was derogated upon the signing of the treaties. The passage of the Indian Act simply compounded this situation. The first Indian Act was passed in 1868. The government soon realized that if they were to make the Indians their wards there must be a special act to govern. I do not propose to review the past Indian acts but simply to consider the parts of the provisions which I have already placed on the record.
In the past undoubtedly special legislation was necessary to protect the Indian but now
Canada Elections Act
thousands of Indians have been to Europe to fight for our country in the second world war and even in the first war. They can read and they do read newspapers; they have radios. They live in a democracy and they would like some of the democracy on their own reserves as well as outside. Hopes ran high among the Indian people that they were at last to get a new act. They hoped-at least a large portion of them-that they would get the vote. They hoped that they would also be able to run their own affairs. Some advantages were given to them by the new act, but actually Indian affairs in most cases are still being run in much the same manner as they were 90 years ago.
The new act really did not give the Indians the vote. The courts have held that an Indian's property, both real and personal, off the reserve is taxable, while on the reserve it is not. Under the Indian Act if he takes the vote he will be taxed on his land and on his personal property on the reserve and he must pay succession and inheritance taxes. The Indian can, with the consent of the minister, apply for enfranchisement and become a Canadian citizen under the present provisions of the Indian Act. If he does that he will then have the vote but he must transfer his land to another Indian on the reserve within 30 days and sell any improvements that he may have made on it. If it is not sold by then it is auctioned off and he must take what he can get for it. Once enfranchised neither he, his wife nor his children can ever return to the reserve. They receive compensation for the income they would have received had they stayed on the reserve for the next 20 years but of course this is much less than the children would have eventually received.
These terms in the present Indian Act make the Indian people themselves-a large portion of them at any rate-dread enfranchisement. These terms, the terms which I suggest the mover of the bill has not taken into consideration in his companion legislation when he proposes certain amendments to the Indian Act, are such that there is not much purpose in the house acceding to this bill being passed when the companion legislation which purports to effect the amendments which are necessary is lacking.
To get back to what enfranchisement would do to the majority of the Indian people resident on the reserves. To the Indian, as I said, enfranchisement is a threat rather than a privilege and the section of the Indian Act which allows an individual or a whole tribe to be forced into enfranchisement without their consent is truly a threat over their heads. It is difficult for an

Canada Elections Act
Indian to give up his only home and the only way o f life he knows to receive the privilege of the vote. With his limited experience he usually feels the price is too high. He cannot foresee that without the vote he will never have a voice in running his own affairs or enacting the laws governing him.
Not only is it extremely difficult for the Indian to obtain the vote, but he also lacks that fundamental right we all cherish, namely the right to own our own property. Off the reserve the Indian may own property but on it he may not. It matters not whether the title for the reserve is held in the name of the crown or whether it is a grant, as long as the property is for the exclusive use of the Indians, it is under the jurisdiction of the department of Indian affairs and from their decision there is no appeal under the present provisions of the act. The minister of the department, before this government came into power, in the past decided what the reserve will be used for; that is, this purpose or that purpose. Under the provisions of the act the minister may decide what portion may be divided into lots or sections, or whether it should be divided at all. He decides-in this case she decides-where roads will run and what portion will be set aside for schools and hospitals.
No Indian may even hold a small portion of his own reserve as his own. If the tribe votes a portion of the reserve to any one Indian the minister may, if she so desires, take the land from that Indian and give it to another. If the minister does take it she will pay to the Indian the amount she decides for the house and any improvements which have been made on the land. Even on the Indian's death his widow cannot stay on the land unless the minister consents to her presence, nor can the Indian's heirs; nor can the Indian lease any portion of the land the tribe may have voted him without the minister's consent. He may, with the consent of the minister and of the whole tribe, surrender his land back to the crown and the minister will then dispose of that land in the manner in which she sees fit. If the whole tribe desires to leave the reserve, they cannot sell their reserve without the minister's consent. The minister may even lease the Indian's land to a white man, if she so desires, for one year, without the Indian's consent.
In the new act there is a section which says that a tribe, if they get the government's consent, can secure control of the land on their reservation and supervise its allotment, but as this consent can be withdrawn at any time it offers little hope to the Indian of ever getting permanent control of his property. The fact that the Indian must always be 
a tenant of the crown discourages him from improving the land or taking pride in it. In other words, the minister and the department have complete control of the land of the Indian people. The Indian, because he has no vote, has no real voice in the appointment of the minister and from the minister's decision there is no appeal.
One does not have to look very far for justification of the principle behind the legislation before the house. Extending to the Indian people the right to exercise the franchise would give them some voice in the actions of the federal government in these matters relating to the disposition of the land which has been preserved for the Indian people by treaties of 100 years ago and more.
These provisions of the Indian Act to which I have referred are only a small portion of the provisions of that act which must be considered as companion amendments to the legislation before the house before the bill should go forward in its present incomplete form, incomplete inasmuch as the companion bill is incomplete, and much more consideration must be given to the matter.
I might refer here to the committee on Indian affairs which has been established and which is composed of members of this house and the other place. At this time that committee is in the process of considering all aspects of the life of the Indian people of Canada. It is a committee that has been wanting for a long time, a committee upon which is sitting a very distinguished member of a well-known Indian band of the west who is also a very distinguished member of the other place. For the first time in Canada's history the Indian people will have a voice of authority on this committee. This is a great stride forward in the achievement of an understanding of the problems confronting the Indian people.
I have no doubt whatever that the enfranchisement of the Canadian Indian will be one of the subjects which will be considered by the joint committee, and perhaps at this juncture it would be proper for me to suggest to members of the house that this bill should not go forward now and, indeed, at any time until the findings of the committee which is now sitting are made known. Undoubtedly the committee will delve very searchingly and deeply into those provisions of the Indian Act to which I have referred during the course of my remarks. Once the committee has done that I am quite certain it will come up with all these factors I have mentioned which have a bearing on the far-reaching results that the passage of this bill would have, having in mind the fact that the bill might conflict with the provisions of

the present Indian Act. As I have already pointed out, quite conceivably substantial disadvantages might accrue to the Canadian Indian people if the bill were to pass in its present form without very searching consideration being given first to all the relevant provisions of the Indian Act.
I wish to make it quite clear before resuming my seat that the Yukon Indian people as well as the Northwest Territories Indian people have the right to vote in federal elections. I would venture to say that that right is cherished by the Indian people of the Yukon. Certainly they would not want to see anything done to disturb it and certainly I would do my utmost to oppose any such move vigorously. Having lived among the Indian people of the Yukon I can assure hon. members that they have as much grasp of the issues involved in federal elections as a good many of their white brothers, and on that score no member of the house should have any hesitation in supporting the principle involved in the bill.
I wish also to make one further point. There are Indian people in this country above the 60th parallel and, indeed, a good number of Eskimo people residing in areas of Canada who have no representation in this house at all. I am speaking of the Indian people who reside east of the 102nd meridian on the mainland of Canada and of the Eskimo people who reside on the Arctic islands. There are some Indian people east of the 102nd meridian. It is my intention to propose in the very near future that this area of Canada, now unrepresented in the house, be included as an electoral district and that the people residing there be given the opportunity of voting in federal elections. They are Canadian citizens as much as any hon. member of this house and as such they are entitled to the same rights and privileges.
I might mention here that by our neglect in not having taken this area into the collective consideration of Canada a large number of white citizens are also deprived of the vote in federal elections. I refer now to Royal Canadian Mounted Police stationed in these areas as well as defence personnel, personnel manning weather stations, scientists and the like. All of these people in this area are disenfranchised because there is simply no representation. However, I think chiefly of the Indian people, the subject of this bill, when I speak of this particular area. In the north there is certainly no doubt that above the 60th parallel all the Indian people cherish the right to vote and, speaking in full support of the principle behind this measure, I wish to suggest to the hon. member who has introduced the legislation that, because of all the reasons I have 66968-9-271
Canada Elections Act
mentioned, the bill should be deferred until the findings of the joint committee of this house and the other place have been made known.

subtopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROTECT VOTING RIGHTS OF INDIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the intent of Bill No. C-13, an act to amend the Canada Elections Act, is to extend the franchise to Indians now living on reservations. As the previous speaker pointed out, the Eskimos of the northern lands, the Indians of the Yukon and Northwest Territories and those Indians who have left reservations have the vote but Indians who are still on reservations, numbering some 165,000 or 170,000, have no vote. Their affairs are managed by government officials under the supervision of a minister of the crown and they have no recourse against that minister's decision through being able to express their pleasure or displeasure by the way they cast their ballots.
The mover of the bill has pointed out that this bill is a companion piece to Bill No. C-15, an act to amend the Indian Act, and that both bills have to be considered together. He has pointed out also that at the present time there are six provinces which extend the vote to Indians on reservations.
In 1949, the province of British Columbia extended the vote to Indians on reservations. In that year, the first native Indian, a Mr. Frank Calder, was elected to the provincial legislature from the constituency of Atlin. Other provinces which have extended the vote to Indians on reservations are Ontario, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, Manitoba and New Brunswick. The history of the Indian nations, who are the original people of Canada, is a proud one. Their loyalty to the crown, their loyalty to Canada, has been unquestioned in wars starting with the war of 1812-14 and continuing through to the second world war.
I can hardly agree with the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) about the difficulties which can be encountered in implementing this bill, and I listened most intently to what he had to say. It seems to me the purpose of the bill is very simple. It simply says the federal government will do what these six provincial governments have done, that is give the Indians on reservations the right to vote without the loss of any of their treaty rights. He has pointed out that at the present time there is a standing committee on privileges and elections which has been set up to consider and recommend revisions to the Canada Elections Act. Undoubtedly the field covered in this bill will be considered by that committee, and for that reason it is perhaps very apt that this bill should come before us now. The debate which has occurred on this bill has covered

Canada Elections Act
most of the aspects of the problem and should provide this committee with a wealth of information when they are considering the revision of the Canada Elections Act.
It has been pointed out also that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has appointed the Hon. James Gladstone, a full-blooded Indian, to the other place. This is the first time that has happened. It does indicate that the government is conscious of the obligation to give our original Canadians representation in the government. I would think the logical follow-up from this point would be to pick out the essence of these two bills, that is Bill No. C-13 and Bill No. C-15, and implement their provisions in the relatively near future.
It has been pointed out also that there is a joint committee of this house and the other place set up to study the Indian Act. It seems to me that we would be ill advised to press either of these measures at the present time until these two committees, which have the power to send for people and to investigate very thoroughly, make their reports to this house. I expect the hon. member who sponsored this bill will be a member of both of those committees. I believe the problem can be cured at that time and some of the difficulties which the previous speaker has foreseen can be overcome as a result of the consideration given to these problems.
In my riding, which is a city riding, I do have an Indian reservation on the western boundary. The Indian children on that reservation attend a school where they mix with white children from a very fine area of the city. I am assured by the principal of that school that these young Indian boys and girls take second place to none in their ability, in their application and in their potential as good citizens of this country. There are numerous examples of the tremendous contributions made by Indians in the development of art, literature, business, finance, and in almost every field of Canadian endeavour. I have no hesitation in saying that I support the idea behind both of these bills. I am most anxious to see what I consider to be an injustice, that is the failure to give Indians a franchise, corrected. I believe that the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) has made a worth while contribution in bringing forward these two bills.

subtopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROTECT VOTING RIGHTS OF INDIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on many previous occasions I have taken part in debates on bills similar to this one dealing with the same objectives as this one has. I compliment the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) for being so persistent in bringing this bill forward in this session

as well as the past several sessions. I do agree with, and I am in sympathy with, the objectives of this bill.
I have the honour to represent the Indian reservation with the largest population in Canada. I refer to the Six Nations reservation near Brantford. Before going farther, however, it might be well to go into the history of the voting privileges of the Indian people in Canada. It is interesting to note that in 1885 a Conservative government gave the Indian people the privilege of voting. This privilege was based on a property qualification, and as near as I can understand it the qualification was that the Indian had to own a house to the value of around $150. This permitted almost any Indian to vote at that time.
It is interesting also to note that in the year 1898 the Liberal government of that day changed the law and made it necessary that the names of the Indians appear on the provincial enumeration lists. Of course I would presume that in 1898 there were very few provinces that permitted Indians to vote, and in that way the vote was taken away from most of the Indian people. After the first world war, of course, the veterans' names were added to the list of those having voting privileges, and after the second world war their spouses were permitted the privilege of voting. This is the position so far as federal elections are concerned now, outside of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
Ontario gave Indian people the privilege to vote in 1953. It is interesting to note the results of that action in the number of votes polled on the Six Nations Indian reservation in the three elections preceding 1953 and the one election that has followed 1953. In 1945, 89 votes were polled on that reservation; that is in the 1945 provincial election. In 1948, 97 votes were polled in the Brant portion and 3 in the Haldimand-Norfolk portion of the reservation, or a total of 100. In the election in 1951, in the Brant portion 89 votes were polled and in Haldimand-Norfolk 15 votes were polled, making a total of 104 votes. In the 1955 election, after the privilege of voting had been extended to the Indians, out of a total of 1,447 names on the list in the Brant section and 209 names on the list in the Haldimand-Norfolk section, it was found that 223 voted in the Brant section and 55 voted in the Haldimand-Norfolk section, making a total of 278 voting out of a possible 1,656.
That is an indication of the result. While not nearly all of those Indian people voted, a considerably larger number voted in the 1955 election than did in the previous elections. As I say, while not nearly all voted, there was a considerable increase in the numbers who did so. We know that all will not

vote. It is against the religion of some of them to vote. Hence, they do not wish to do so for anything.
The Indian people of Canada, being the first citizens of this country should be entitled to the same right and privileges as other citizens. I have said that on many occasions. A high percentage of those on the Six Nations reservation served in both world war I and world war II. They fought for their country. They are interested in the affairs of the country. As they became educated more fully over a number of years I think perhaps they will take a greater interest if given the privilege of voting.
It has been said that this proposal is trying to force the vote on the Indian people. I am sure there is no such intention. No one else in Canada is forced to vote. Why should the Indians be forced to vote either? As I said before, as to some of the people, namely those who retain their original religion and who are known as pagan Indians, it is against their religion to vote for anything; and, of course, they will not vote for the council on the reservations. You could not expect them to vote if it is against their principles to do so. But as time goes on the situation may change. I might say here that the educational system on that Six Nations reservation at or near Brantford is far better than that of most townships in that vicinity.
Some fear the loss of some of their privileges if they vote. Among those privileges, of course, would be the right not to pay taxes on the reservation. Indians, of course, pay all other taxes anyway except the personal income tax on money earned on the reservation and property tax on the reservation. They also enjoy a dual citizenship as between Canada and the United States. They fear that if they voted in a Canadian election they might lose that dual citizenship. I am sure they would not do so, but if they feel that way it is rather hard to convince them otherwise.
We have an Indian affairs committee set up to study the problems of the Indian people. I am sure that committee will go into this problem fully within the next year or so and I am sure that they will find a solution to this problem. Although, as I said before, I am in thorough agreement with the principle of this bill, I feel that it would perhaps be better if it were left over until after this committee has sat, completed its deliberations and brought forward its recommendations. I am sure that something will come out of its study. In view of the fact that many provinces now give the Indians a vote, probably something will be done with respect to the federal elections act. I am happy 66968-9-271J

to have had the opportunity to take part in this debate. I hope that something constructive will come out of the committee hearings.

subtopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROTECT VOTING RIGHTS OF INDIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened to hon. members who have spoken previously on Bill No. C-15, I felt possibly they were speaking from experiences in their own constituencies. I think we must all make a contribution on the basis of the experience we have gained. While it is obvious that a great deal of research has been done, especially by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), and while certainly my contribution will not compare with his in erudition, I might admit to some close ties with the Indian people. I refer not to blood ties but to social ties. My father was able to speak the Cree language when he was a young man and went to school with the Indians some seventy years ago. The school at that time was in the Qu'Appelle valley and was integrated probably seventy years before its time. However, I just wanted to give the background for my contribution.
We must deal with Indians of many different types and temperaments. The need for the franchise must possibly be analysed at a local level. In this situation we must face some cold hard facts. It seems to me that there are some things which the Indian needs much more than he needs the franchise. In the next few minutes I intend to introduce some facts which will bear out that statement. In the province of Saskatchewan last year, in the Qu'Appelle valley there was a large gathering of Indian representatives. While in the process of discussing the affairs of the Indians they were met by a delegation of the provincial government led by the premier of that province. The premier at that time offered the franchise to the Indians and the right to buy liquor. I can say, Mr. Speaker, that 95 per cent of the Indians on the committee rejected the proposal. In the light of a decision of that nature we cannot be too hasty in suggesting that those Indians would prefer to have the franchise.
I think it has been found that the Indian is still afraid of losing his treaty rights. We have been unable to convince the Indian that we are not putting his inherent rights in jeopardy when we offer him the franchise. A great many Indians are still unwilling to accept the full responsibility which is assumed by the enfranchised citizen. We must realize that with privileges go responsibilities. We cannot withhold from the Indians the voting privilege when they are willing to accept their full responsibility.

Canada Elections Act
We as legislators have the responsibility to encourage every worthwhile piece of legislation in order that the Indian will be integrated; but, as I mentioned before, the situation must be analysed possibly at a local level. When I look at the situation in my own area I do wonder what is the best plan. The Indians like many other people are having difficulties. Our Indians are experiencing the pangs of growing pains in learning how to conduct their affairs of local administration along the same lines as other citizens. A great advancement is taking place, we must admit, but they are still a long way from being able to legislate for themselves.
As I mentioned in dealing with the local situation with which I am possibly more familiar, and reverting to the point which I made about the Indian getting something more than a franchise, I would remind the house that on a reservation of possibly 300 families only 120 of these are engaged in farming and the raising of livestock. The remainder of those families make their living or are sustained by old age assistance income, casual labour, domestic labour and by the sale of hay and other available products on their reservation. The other 180 families are living on the bounty of the government. When we have Indians in that situation, we wonder whether there is some more helpful means of bringing them along into integration than merely by the franchise.
Again looking at it from a local level, we must realize that we have different groups of Indians even on the one reservation or in the one tribe. First of all we have the older group, and many of these are bewildered people who cannot understand the technical and social advances and will always be for the rest of their natural lives a charge on society. We wonder what advantage the franchise would be to them. We have the middle aged group with a limited form of education and probably very little technical knowledge. Sometimes they are apathetic to self-government and they have, as I say, little technical knowledge. This, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced is a result of living under a welfare state. As a result of living in this situation we cannot analyse the reaction of the Indian toward the franchise. We cannot comprehend how an Indian of this type will treat his right to vote and become a citizen in the same way as other citizens. We have possibly as the most enlightened group the students of today, and certainly it is a great deal of encouragement to all of us to see the progress which is being made in the academic institutions. Only recently I attended a graduation at the school of the Oblate fathers and saw a group of young Indians

graduate, and they would do credit to any school in Canada. It seems to me that education is certainly the means by which we can place the Indian in a position where he will be able to appreciate the franchise and exercise it to the best of his ability.
We see as time goes on in the department of indian affairs that Indians are receiving the right to look after their own affairs. They are being given more responsibility, and only recently I noticed in my own area that several have been placed in positions as assistant farm instructors. In this type of development naturally the time will come when the Indians will be able to look after themselves, and I believe it is only a matter of time until the Indians of Canada will be in the position to accept in its full meaning the right to vote, the franchise which we all enjoy, and until the Indians themselves are ready and willing to accept that responsibility, I do not feel it should be thrust upon them.

Because I spoke so strongly on the principle involved in this clause on second reading I should like to say a word or two about it. I said that the clause in the bill as printed and presented to the committee was in that form most offensive and could lead to a great many difficulties that would be damaging to the country in certain circumstances. The minister has now come forward with an amendment which, while it does not do all the things we asked in that it does not permit a decision by parliament on the question of whether or not oil import control should be established before such action is taken, it does go a long way in ameliorating the difficulty of which we complained. Because it goes such a long way I think it is perfectly proper to accept it as a compromise. It can, I think we must admit, be argued that it is a wholly reasonable compromise of two conflicting points of view and it certainly will permit the minister to take action to have the government provide for the possible difficulties of which he thought there was some danger and for which he thought provision should be made. At the same time it permits parliamentary control over the action even although that parliamentary control may be a second-class method in that it comes after the action has taken place.
Since it is put forward as a compromise and does go a long way toward meeting the difficulty we raised at the earlier stages of this bill, I am perfectly content to accept it, and I must acknowledge to the minister our appreciation of his bringing it forward. Possibly, there are some small objections which could be taken to subclause 3, but those are guarded against by the fact that it is limited to oil only. It is possible to make out a hypothetical case against it but I think legislation has to be practical. While our objections to the clause 85 (2) as it existed before that subclause was deleted stands in its full force and vigour, I think having the clause limited as it is here to oil removes most of the objections to it, or sufficient of them that we are not going to press the matter further.

speechtext:
I think this is a rather unusual clause. As the hon. member for Ottawa West has pointed out, there are four other clauses of the bill which deal with regulations that may be made by the board, in some instances with the approval of the governor in council, or as in clause 7 without the approval of the governor in council. Clause 88, of course, is one that hardly touches the kind of purpose that the minister stated conceivably could belong to clause 89. But certainly, clause 7 in particular and clause 42 would seem to embrace what might be contemplated in clause 89, in order to make effective the purposes and provisions of this act.
One wonders certainly whether this clause is needed at all. I am particularly impressed with this observation made by the hon. member for Ottawa West. When you look at clause 7 the board may, under that clause, make rules without any reference to the governor in council with respect to the sittings of the board; with respect to matters having to do with the procedure in relation to applications, representations and complaints made to the board; the conduct of the hearings before the board; the manner and conduct of any business before the board. Likewise, in subclause (c), the board may make rules, again without reference to the governor in council, with regard to the division of work amongst the members, the assignment of hearings and so on. I suppose

that means, as the minister said the other night, amongst the various members of the board, and this was the argument he used, in part, for a five-man board as opposed to a three-man board. The clause refers to the assignment to members of the board of various responsibilities with regard to hearings.
Then, subclause (d) is so general as to be almost synonymous with the intent of the language in clause 89, that is to say, generally carrying on the work of the board, the management of its internal affairs, duties of its officers and employees. Now, what point is there in keeping clause 89 unless it is clear that the purposes intended and the objectives covered in that clause are different from the powers given for making regulations in the four cited clauses. It is conceivable that there may be a conflict between regulations drawn up by the board, either on its autonomous authority as provided for in clause 7 or after having received the approval of the governor in council. The governor in council may decide upon particular regulations and the board may decide upon another set of regulations, and there would be a conflict. There is nothing in this act, unless I am unmindful of the earlier provisions, which would give priority in law to those regulations drawn up under clause 89 by the governor in council.
It seems to us, in the absence of more precise information, that there could be no reason for this clause. Another objection to this clause, I believe, is that there is no limitation on the extent of time it may run. It could easily be argued by the governor in council that for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of this act the regulations must be not only those enacted by the governor in council at the beginning but regulations which the governor in council might, from time to time, in the long future enact. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the legislation we are now discussing and which has been discussed before, on various occasions in this house, is the federal-provincial tax-sharing arrangements act.

Tonight, and before coming to the particular section mentioned in the bill, i.e. clause 12, I would like to deal to some extent with certain general principles connected with the sharing of taxes between the provinces and federal government.
The fiscal problem now existing between the federal government and the provinces, Mr. Speaker, is both very significant and very simple.
It is very significant because, it is a basic aspect of our constitution, and also because one of the main sources of financing the provincial and federal governments depends on its being solved.
The problem is also very simple to my mind, except for those who want to confuse the issue in order to be able to say later that it cannot be solved, at least for the present. There are also those perfectionists who agree to consider drastic and permanent solutions only. They should, however, realize that it is impossible to have such solutions accepted, and that their unbending attitude frequently remains sterile and prevents any gradual improvement, which very often is the only one possible.
All serious-minded people, who have made the effort to study those arrangements and to consider the over-all aspect of the matter will admit today that, according to our constitution, the federal and the provincial governments have concurrent rights in the field of direct taxation. There are not-though some people will maintain there are-any priority rights in this field; such rights, indeed, cannot exist without limitation, as otherwise they would lead up, through their exercise, to exclusive powers. In fact, if, for instance, the provinces had a right to some priority, or else, if they had a priority right to direct taxation, such priority would not necessarily stop at 50 per cent, nor at 75 per cent of that source of taxation; it could go as far as 100 per cent and, indeed, it would then become an exclusive right.
Our constitution therefore provides for concurrent rights in that field, and even if some of us wish that it be otherwise, I am convinced that this aspect of our constitution will not change in the near future. I am convinced, and the experience of the past proves it-the experience of the past is conclusive in that regard-that neither the federal government nor the provinces will agree to surrender the rights which the con-
Dominion-Provincial Relations stitution recognize as being theirs in the field of direct taxation. Those who seek a solution of such a sweeping nature to the fiscal problem lack realism or sincerity. Contending to aim at perfection, as they see it, and which is impossible of achievement, they do not seek to achieve improvements which, indeed, would be possible.
Therefore, faced with those consequences and in presence of the situation as we find it today, we must accept, in a practical way, the existence of those concurrent rights. Such is, in my opinion, the basic fact at the root of the whole fiscal problem.
Another fundamental aspect of that matter is the fact that the federal government and the provinces will wish to go on exercising concurrent rights. Besides, the very exercise of those concurrent rights, without any limitation or corrective action, would end up in a double taxation pattern which would become excessive and would lead to unacceptable regional discrimination, in view of the highly different returns from direct income in the various provinces. Now, we know, by experience, that all Canadians, in every province, are opposed to double taxation which would result in adding unduly' to the taxpayers' burden, but on the other hand, they support the steps taken by the federal government to equalize the yield of direct taxes as between the various provinces.
Out of this general desire of Canadians, there arise two basic considerations underlying any practical solution to the fiscal problem. In view of the fact, as I said earlier, that both the federal government and the provinces can be expected to continue exercising their concurrent rights in the field of direct taxes, there must be specific arrangements between both levels of government so as to mitigate, and if possible to avoid, the problems involved in double taxation. Furthermore, such arrangements should provide for a system of equalization payments as a means of equalizing the tax yield between the provinces, through a redistribution of tax revenues for the benefit of the less favoured provinces, so that such provinces too may face their constitutional responsibilities.
From these findings, Mr. Speaker, there arise two definite requirements. I should like to discuss both these requirements which, I think are of equal importance in this discussion. First, there must be fiscal arrangements as between the federal government and the provinces, to enable both levels of government to exercise their rights, while avoiding as much as possible the
4274	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations serious problems involved in double taxation. Second, such fiscal arrangements must involve equalization payments, because otherwise, tax revenues will be neither lair nor equitable.
But there is more. I do not think it is possible, nor indeed desirable, that either the federal government or the provinces should accept a limitation in the exercise of their constitutional taxation rights. The sovereignty of those governments and the flexibility that is so necessary to a fiscal policy, especially in a federal state, are inconsistent with such limitation. But then, if fiscal arrangements should not be such as to limit taxation rights of both types of government, other than the limits already set out in our constitution, the only practical result that we could expect of such arrangements is the establishment of a reasonable area within which the provinces could exercise their taxation rights, while avoiding double taxation and an increased tax burden for the taxpayers.
It is in that way that the main purpose of the fiscal arrangements is to fix the limits within which double taxation will be avoided, but those arrangements should in no way limit the right for the exercise of this right by the parties concerned, that is, the provincial and federal governments.
I submit that all the basic requirements of an acceptable and practical solution of the taxation problem were met in the fiscal arrangements introduced under the government of the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent.
Those unquestionable merits were recognized by Mr. Drew himself when in 1956, speaking in the house, on the bill then before parliament, he said the following as found in Hansard of July 16, 1956, page 5993; I quote:
(Text):
-I wish to make it quite clear that the present formula has some merits in the acceptance of certain very important principles. As the minister pointed out, the proposal contemplates the continuance of a form of tax rental agreement, arrangements for federal collection of payments under those agreements, a tax equalization plan, a provincial stabilization fund which will protect municipalities against a severe drop in their revenues, and in turn an abatement in the federal taxation fields of personal income, corporation taxes and succession duties. The acceptance by the federal government of the place of the provinces and the right of the provinces in the field of income tax, corporation tax, succession duties and other direct taxes is, in itself, a welcome evidence of a return to the position which was always accepted without question over the years between 1867 and 1941, when the wartime tax agreements were signed.
(Translation):
Those were the words spoken by the leader of the opposition at the time. Even Mr. 

Duplessis who, you will agree, I am sure, Mr. Speaker, since you have a wealth of experience in politics, even Mr. Duplessis, who is not easily satisfied when making requests of others, stated at the end of the conference in March 1956 that the solution suggested by the federal government of the day was a great step in the right direction. However many of his followers in this house are still bitterly critical of the spirit and the substance of the arrangements then introduced. Criticism is easy, of course, especially when it is vague and when it is voiced from a particular standpoint. But I still have to hear in this house any of those hon. Conservative members from Quebec make a concrete proposal Which stands the least chance of being accepted by the government concerned.
Mr. Speaker, they are opposed to the substance and to the very principle of the present arrangements. The Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) stated in the house, on October 18, 1956, that he was still opposed to the subsidies derived from the present fiscal arrangements, and that the fiscal proposals which would be submitted by the Conservative government, during the conference held in November 1957, would have a basis quite different from the one on which was predicated the formula put forward by the Liberals. However, the province of Quebec is still receiving this year, in 1959, about $55 million from the federal government in the way of subsidies which the Solicitor General described as ultra vires when he sat on this side of the house, in the opposition.
As for the Conservative members from Quebec who were elected for the first time in March, on March 31, 1958, to be accurate, they must remember that during the last election campaign they bitterly denounced the present fiscal arrangements as recognizing the theft by the federal government of provincial taxation rights. They must also recall that they took the solemn undertaking to denounce these fiscal arrangements and to see to it that the constitution be complied with. They now have the opportunity to carry out their solemn pledge to the Quebec voters and they cannot do it any other way than by voting against this motion whose fundamental aim is to extend the very fiscal arrangements that they condemned, and to come up with another formula. I hope, Mr. Speaker that they will have the courage to carry out their solemn pledge.

It was easy for them to make such statements in the province of Quebec during the last election. This is the place and now is the time for them to fight, here in parliament, on that bill now before us, and to show that they have the courage that befits honest and sincere people.
So far, in this debate, they have been conspicuous by their silence. We have heard but a single speech, very brief and very mild, by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn).
Is that how they mean to fight the great battle for autonomy? They will not always be able to escape their responsiblities by remaining silent. When the time comes for them to vote on the principle of this bill, I hope that they will not have the cowardice to leave the house as they did on that occasion that we all know about, and to abstain from voting. But then if they stay here, they will have to make a choice: either they will vote against the bill in order to keep their solemn pledge, or they will have to admit that they made a mistake before the last election and that thereby they have misled the voters of the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Whatever the hon. Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) may think, public life also requires the respect of the pledged word. Those hon. Conservative members from the province of Quebec might say, in self-defence, that they have not changed their position, but that they want to support this bill pending the introduction by this government of a better formula. It is in this way, for instance, that the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) has justified here the new position he has taken on the matter of grants to universities.
However, such an attitude is not only wrong, it is unacceptable. To my mind, such an attitude cannot be countenanced, neither by us who are aware of the situation nor by those to whom promises were made. Mr. Speaker, when some legislation allegedly violates a country's constitution, when such arrangement is held to be an usurpation of provincial constitutional powers, when anybody states his opposition in principle to any bill, he cannot decently favour the legislation by merely waiting, under the pretext that in some hazy future, a more acceptable formula might turn up.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
As a matter of fact, even that unjustifiable pretext cannot be advanced under the circumstances, because it is clear that the government is not attempting to improve fiscal arrangements in the manner indicated by Conservative members from Quebec before the last election. As a matter of fact, by failing, as we have tried to point out on many occasions on this side of the house, to call a real conference of premiers, which could take decisions in this matter, and by organizing a series of meetings of officials who cannot even discuss the true issues, because they have not enough authority to do so, the government reveals its desire to multiply delays, without seeking a new solution, so as to avoid too much embarrassment to certain provincial premiers.
It is indeed rather improbable, Mr. Speaker, that an entirely new solution can be found which would be acceptable to all the governments concerned, or even that fundamental aspects of the present fiscal arrangements might be improved, in view of the divergent interests and attitudes of the various provinces and the federal government. From the viewpoint of the provinces, the best way to improve those arrangements would, as I said a few moments ago, consist in widening the area within which provincial governments may apply their rights of direct taxation without resorting to double taxation. Besides, that is the kind of improvement that all provincial premiers did propose, except, of course, Mr. Duplessis, who proposed nothing definite at the conference of November 1957, which, as we all know, was adjourned after two days, and it is the kind of improvement that the federal government refuses, in spite of everything and everybody, notwithstanding the requests made from this side of the house, to reconvene the provinces in order to discuss and consider that matter.
As we know, the field within which the provinces may exercise their rights without imposing double taxation, amounted last year to 13 per cent of the personal income tax, to 9 per cent of profits, or about 24 per cent of the corporation federal tax and finally, to 50 per cent of federal estate tax. It should not be overlooked, however, and that is the important point, that the rate of 13 per cent on personal income tax does not change every year with the rate of the federal tax. Under present arrangements, it is 13 per cent of the federal tax, as determined in 1956, so that the field of taxation exclusively entrusted to the provinces increases as the federal tax decreases, but it decreases, on the other hand, as the federal tax increases.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
During the 1957 election campaign the Conservative party promised to treat both the provinces and the municipalities with generosity. It pledged itself, on behalf of the federal government, to vacate a greater part of the direct taxation field, in order to allow the provinces to better utilize that source of income without increasing the total burden of taxation.
We recall that the arrangements, as set up by the Liberals, were on the basis of 10-9-50, but that the premier of Ontario, who claimed he was certain to obtain what he wanted if the Conservatives came into power in 1957, demanded a 15-15-50 arrangement. But what happened, Mr. Speaker? In January 1958, the Conservative government, facing a new election, took a very timid step in the direction it had promised to follow, and raised from 10 to 13 per cent the provincial share of the federal tax on personal incomes.
Today, the government puts forward a measure aimed merely at extending for a further year the arrangement made in 1958. That is the purpose of the amendment now before the house.
However, there is another angle to the situation, and it is one which should not be overlooked, because it does reveal the present government's true attitude on the problem of sharing direct taxes. Last year, as I said, the provinces received 13 per cent of the federal tax on personal incomes, in accordance with the figure set in 1956. On the other hand, the federal government this year increased the rate of its tax on personal incomes, and as a result will be receiving, on an annual basis, approximately $130 million more than last year. However, the share of the provinces remains the same, because it is still based on the year 1956. The upshot of all this is that in 1959-60, the federal government will be increasing its share of the tax on personal incomes over last year's figure and, as a result, the provinces will have to be satisfied with a much smaller share than last year in that field of taxation.
However, that is not all. It will be recalled that under the tax arrangements introduced by the Liberals, 9 per cent of corporation profits went to the provinces, while 38 per cent of those profits went to the federal government. The provincial share was therefore about 24 per cent of the federal share. The Conservatives made no change to that

situation last year. This year, however, the federal government raised the tax on corporation profits by 3 points. Now, what does this mean? It means that the share granted exclusively to the provinces remains at 9 per cent of profits, whereas the federal government share is now raised to 41 per cent. The provincial share in this field, therefore, is now only 22 per cent of the federal share.
Before the 1958 election, the federal government had thus done something in favour of the provinces. But that like so many other things done by this government, was to a very large extent purely electoral and, once the election was over, the federal government quickly took to a course diametrically opposite to the one that it had solemnly pledged to follow.
I do say now-and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) himself will correct me if I am wrong-that the federal government will receive this year a larger proportion of the revenues from direct taxation than it would have received on the basis of the taxation rates established by the former federal administration.
It is true that we must not expect the Conservative government to do all it has pledged to do during its first years of administration. We already have heard that we should learn to wait. We should learn to be patient. But we have a right to ask, at least, that the government aim its policy in the direction that it has pledged to follow. Well, it is precisely the contrary that is happening now. Having pledged to aim its policy in this direction, the government follows another course. How can we trust a government that says one thing and acts differently? And, I might add, not only in the field of taxation, but in many other fields. How can the government be sincere in organizing meetings, the sole purpose of which can only be to give more room to the provinces in the field of direct taxation, when it decides, even before those meetings are held, to take a larger share in this field?
In fact, the new attitude of the federal government in the field of federal-provincial relations becomes increasingly clear since the budget speech of the Minister of Finance. As I have said earlier, the Minister of Finance has announced at that time that he would take from now on a larger share of the revenues from direct taxation. Such is the inevitable effect of the tax increases which were then decreed.

However, the Minister of Finance has gone further, he has decreed his own new formula. Here is a statement he made in a speech delivered at the Seigniory Club on May 26 last:
(Text):
One reason for bringing the budget this year into better balance was our desire to reduce the heavy pressure of new federal government borrowings on the bond market and on the interest rate structure and to leave more for essential financing by provincial and municipal governments and business.
(Translation):
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance then stated that the federal government had decided to levy further taxes in order to allow municipalities and provinces to borrow more. Such is the new deal the Conservative government suggested to the provinces at that time. The government tells them: "Borrow,-borrow more; as for me, I shall tax". The government takes up more space in the taxation field so as to leave municipalities and provinces a wider range in the borrowing field. What it doesn't say, however, is that it is not costing the government any more to tax more, while thanks to its monetary policy, borrowing becomes every day more costly to the provinces and the municipalities.
As may be noted, Mr. Speaker, the election promises made by the Conservative party in the field of fiscal relations in 1957 and 1958 have been completely disallowed. The Conservative government, far from treating the provinces with more generosity than did the Liberals, as it had promised, takes over a greater share of direct taxation. It completely ignores the concrete proposals put forward by the majority of provincial premiers in November 1957. More than that, it even refuses to meet them again.
It is for all those reasons that the Conservative members from Quebec should now have the courage of their convictions and denounce such betrayal. They must do so, in the name of their principles; they must do so on account of the solemn pledge they made during the last federal election; they must do so for the sake of their electors to whom they gave that pledge, but they must do so also, and perhaps above all, on account of Mr. Duplessis, who is responsible for their presence here in the house.

subtopic: NATIONAL MUSEUM
NATIONAL MUSEUM
subsubtopic: NON-CANADIAN SCIENTIFIC PERSONNEL
speechtext:
1.	Have any of the scientific personnel employed at the national museum of Canada since 1935, not held British or Canadian citizenship at the time of their appointment?
2.	If so, what were their names and the positions they held at the museum, in what country were they born and of what country were they citizens at the time of their appointment, for what period did each hold a position at the museum and for what reason was their employment terminated?
3.	From what universities did each hold degrees, and what positions had each held prior to his or her employment by the national museum of Canada?
4.	Were any of these appointments to the museum made through the usual civil service competition?
5.	If so, which persons were so appointed, on what date, did the civil service competition take place, and of what country was each person a citizen at the time they made application for employment under this competition?
6.	Were any of these appointments to the museum staff not made through the usual civil service competition?
7.	If so, which persons were not so appointed, on whose recommendation and by what authority were they appointed, and on what date were they appointed?
8.	Did any of the above personnel subsequently take out Canadian citizenship papers after their appointment to the museum staff?
